This includes topics such as the partition coefficient, phase fraction during solidification, and liquid feeding by way of dendrite coherency. 2 1 Introduction Fundamental phase relationships and thermophysical properties are very often the first sets of information referenced by metallurgical and materials engineers when making product and process design decisions. That prominence is indicative of the importance of complete and accurate reference materials for both immediate needs and to anticipate future use. While technique limitations, unrecognized sources of error, and usually simple, but meaningful mistakes will always keep metallurgists yearning for higher accuracy, the shear size and scope of metallurgical property investigation is more often the limiting factor. Since uranium is used more narrowly than, for instance, aluminum or iron alloys, the lower total volume of research by comparison easily leads to more persistent gaps in property knowledge. Material properties change with temperature, composition, and phase with the detailed expression of the measurements being strongly influenced by the volume fraction, morphology and topology of constituent phases. Spread across 67 of the more frequently encountered uranium binary systems1, as enumerated from Kassner and Peterson (1995), there are at least 127 uranium intermetallics (+21 metastable or suspected phases), 7 systems with extended solubility that undergo further reactions without intermetallic phases, and an additional 21 with broad ranges of liquid immiscibility. Consideration of multinary systems increases the complexity further. Moving from highly controlled laboratory conditions to manufacturing reality nearly always requires additional degrees of approximation, extrapolation and assumption due to the further expanding set of interacting variables.
